newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran attacks mock enemy in largest Gulf wargames.
newsitem.headline: Iran attacks mock enemy in largest Gulf wargames.

text.p: Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked an imaginary enemy in the Gulf on Thursday with ground, naval and air power in mock battles in the Islamic republic's largest wargames.

Iranian television, broadcasting live from a coastal area near the port of Bandar Abbas at the mouth of the Gulf, showed missile launches followed by an assault by artillery and armoured units with tanks and ground troops.

Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who has been in the strategic port since the start of the games on Tuesday, watched the operations with the guards' commander, Major-General Mohsen Rezaei, who said they were successful.
Also watching -- from a discreet distance -- was the U.S. Navy.
"We are obviously watching this exercise like we do with all Iranian exercises in the Gulf very closely to keep an eye on their operations," a U.S. Navy official in the Gulf said.
He would not specify what the navy, which keeps a force of about 20 warships in the Gulf to enforce sanctions against Iraq and protect Gulf Arab oil producers, was seeing.
But he dismissed a Tehran report that U.S. warships had left regions near Iranian waters since the start of the wargames.
"We have changed nothing," the U.S. Navy official said. "As at any time during an exercise we are watching it very closely and we can do that in a variety of means, not just ships.
"The Fifth Fleet has not changed its operations as a result of the exercise. As of this morning there are still 20 ships assigned to the Fifth Fleet," he told Reuters.

The official said the number had changed by two or three ships due to routine force rotations. The carrier Theodore Roosevelt finished an exercise on Thursday with the Egyptian air force which had been planned for several months and was now in the Mediterranean with the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

"But we are still conducting maritime intercept operations supporting U.N. sanctions, we're still conducting our routine exercises with other countries, and we haven't changed our operating pattern at all."
The amphibious wargames, codenamed "Tariq ol-Qods" (Road to Jerusalem), involve 200,000 members of the guards -- defenders of Iran's Islamic revolution -- and Basij militia volunteers.
Planned since last year, they are designed to test ability to counter simultaneous threats in Iran's west and south.
They cover 2,000 km (1,240 miles) across four provinces stretching from the mouth of the Gulf to the border with Iraq, Iran's enemy in an eight-year war which ended in 1988.

Saudi Arabia and the other oil-rich monarchies on the Arab side of the Gulf are suspicious of Iran and alarmed by an Iranian military buildup despite Tehran's assurances it is defensive. They have accused Iran of interfering in their internal affairs, a charge denied by Tehran.
